claims.text: The initial alloy has the nominal composition Ta20Nb20Hf20Zr20Ti20.
The conventionally melted and cast Ta20Nb20Hf20Zr20Ti20 alloy is single-phase.
A trace amount of carbon is introduced during alloy synthesis.
Carbon addition followed by aging will promote carbide precipitation.
Solution treatment followed by aging at approximately 600 °C for 2 hours in an inert atmosphere can produce the intended precipitate structure.
Optimized carbon content and aging will produce uniformly dispersed nanoscale carbide precipitates.
The precipitates may be M6C or similar carbon-rich phases.
The carbide precipitates will occur both along grain boundaries and within grains.
Nanoscale carbide precipitates will hinder dislocation motion.
Nanoscale carbide precipitates will hinder grain-boundary sliding.
Hindering dislocation motion and grain-boundary sliding will lower room-temperature creep.
The carbide-containing microstructure will reduce active sites for localized corrosive attack.
Reducing active corrosion sites will create a more chemically stable and passivated microstructure.
The intervention will increase yield strength relative to the untreated alloy.
The intervention will improve room-temperature creep resistance relative to the untreated alloy.
The intervention will improve corrosion resistance relative to the untreated alloy.
The benefits require sufficiently controlled carbon content and aging parameters to retain nanoscale precipitates.
Excessive carbon or improper aging could produce coarse carbides.
Coarse carbides could cause embrittlement and negate the proposed benefits.
An improvement greater than approximately 10% in strength or creep rate is only a speculative estimate.

contradictions.description: The stated baseline receives casting and solution treatment but no aging is specified, whereas the no-carbon control in the experiment is subjected to the same aging treatment as the carbon-containing samples. These are different comparator processing histories.
